lessons.title: ஆனால் / ஆனா (āṉāl / āṉā) — the two Tamils
lessons.gloss: Tamil is two languages at once — the one that is written and the one that is spoken

segments.text: Read மற்றது. Then ask a shopkeeper the price.

blocks.title: Grammar lens: one language, two forms, and everybody uses both

segments.text: Something has been happening quietly in the last eight chapters, and it is time it was said plainly.

Tamil comes in two forms. One is written — in books, on signs, in the news. The other is spoken — at home, in a shop, on a bus. They are not an accent apart. Words differ, and endings differ, and a page of one is not a recording of the other.
Every Tamil speaker uses both and knows which is which. Nobody chooses one and abandons the other.
You have already met three pairs, one per chapter:

That is not a coincidence of these particular words. Joining words are where the split shows most, because they are said constantly and worn down fastest — the same reason an English speaker says cos far more often than because.
It reaches ordinary words too: இன்று, the written today, is இன்னிக்கி in speech.
The single most important fact about Tamil, and a reason the last eight chapters gave you two forms of everything.

segments.source: [YOU RETURN TO: say *alladu* and *-um pōdu* — two distances back — then say which of the two Tamils each one belongs to]

segments.text: Does a Tamil speaker pick one of the two forms and keep to it? (No — everyone uses both, in different places.)

lessons.title: என்று / -ன்னு (eṉṟu / -ṉṉu) — which one you are being taught
lessons.gloss: which of the two this book teaches, and how to hear the other one

segments.text: Ask a price. Then say but twice — the written way, then the spoken way.

blocks.title: Grammar lens: the headword is the written one, on purpose

segments.text: In every lesson of this book, the big word at the top is the written form, and the spoken clip is named beside it in the text. That choice is worth explaining, because it is not obvious.

The written form is the one on the page you will read, the sign you will pass and the form your dictionary will list. It is also understood everywhere Tamil is spoken, which no single spoken variety is.
And it runs one way. From என்று you can predict -ன்னு; from -ன்னு alone you could not have rebuilt என்று. Learn the longer one and the shorter one comes free.
Same sentence. The quotation does not move, the verb does not move; the joining word shrinks onto the word in front of it.
So: say either. Expect to hear the clipped one nearly always, and read the full one nearly always.
You know which Tamil is in front of you, and you can get from one to the other.

segments.instruction: take ēṉeṉṟāl and say the clip; take ēṉṉā and rebuild the full word
segments.source: [YOU CONVERT: take *ēṉeṉṟāl* and say the clip; take *ēṉṉā* and rebuild the full word]

segments.source: [YOU RECALL: read **மற்றது**, then ask *vilai evvaḷavu?*, then say both forms of the quotation line]

segments.instruction: say mēlē, read ஆனால் and say maṟṟadu — three distances back — then say which of the two Tamils each one belongs to
segments.source: [YOU RETURN TO: say *mēlē*, read **ஆனால்** and say *maṟṟadu* — three distances back — then say which of the two Tamils each one belongs to]

segments.text: Why does this book put the written form at the top? (Because the spoken form follows from it, and not the other way round.)
